title: Biology, damage patterns and identification of pests

lessons.title: Pest biology and why it matters
lessons.html:
Know the enemy

Effective control depends on understanding how a pest lives. Its life cycle tells you which stage to target; its habits tell you where to look and where to place treatments; its needs tell you which conditions to change. Treating without this knowledge often fails.

Insect life cycles

  • Complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult): beetles such as the maize weevil and red flour beetle, moths such as the Indian meal moth, flies and fleas. Larvae often cause most damage and may be hidden inside kernels or timber, protected from contact sprays.
  • Incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult): cockroaches, termites and bed bugs. Nymphs look like small adults and live in the same places.

Development speed depends strongly on temperature and moisture. Warm, humid conditions in a South African summer can produce a new generation of stored product insects within weeks, which is why infestations can explode quickly in unmanaged silos.

Rodents

The three main commensal rodents are the Norway (brown) rat, the roof (black) rat and the house mouse. They breed throughout the year where food is available, are neophobic or curious to different degrees, and need to gnaw constantly because their incisors keep growing. Rats generally need access to water; mice can survive on moisture from food.

Other pests

  • Birds such as feral pigeons, sparrows and mynas foul product and structures with droppings and nests.
  • Mites infest damp stored products and can cause allergic reactions.
  • Weeds and invader plants have reproductive strategies such as long-lived seed banks or root suckering that determine control timing.
  • Fungi in stored grain produce heating, mustiness and potentially mycotoxins.

Basic needs

All pests need food, water, shelter and suitable temperature. Removing any of these through sanitation, moisture control, proofing or cooling is the foundation of long-term control.

lessons.title: Recognising damage patterns and signs
lessons.html:
Reading the evidence

Pests are often hidden or nocturnal, so officers usually identify them from signs before seeing the pest itself.

Stored product insects

SignLikely cause
Round exit holes in whole kernelsInternal feeders such as weevils, lesser grain borer
Floury dust and damaged kernel surfacesExternal feeders such as flour beetles, often after primary damage
Silk webbing and clumped kernels on the surfaceMoth larvae such as Indian meal moth
Heating, moisture migration, crustingInsect activity and/or mould in a section of the bulk

Rodents

  • Droppings: Norway rat droppings are larger and blunt-ended, roof rat droppings spindle-shaped, mouse droppings small and pointed. Fresh droppings are soft and dark.
  • Gnaw marks on wood, plastic, cables and bags.
  • Smear marks: greasy rub marks along regular runways.
  • Burrows in soil along walls and under slabs, typical of Norway rats.
  • Tracks in dust, urine stains and odour.

Wood destroying organisms

  • Subterranean termites: earthen mud tubes on walls and foundations, hollowed timber with soil-filled galleries.
  • Wood borer beetles: small round or oval exit holes with fine powdery frass.
  • Wood decay fungi: soft, discoloured, cracked or stringy timber, often where moisture is present.

Health and nuisance pests

  • Cockroaches: droppings like pepper specks or smears, egg cases, musty odour.
  • Bed bugs: small dark spots on mattress seams, cast skins, bites reported in rows.
  • Flies: breeding in decaying organic matter, spotting on surfaces.
  • Birds: droppings, nests, feathers and blocked gutters.

Avoid jumping to conclusions

Different pests can cause similar signs, and old damage may not mean current activity. Confirm whether evidence is fresh and, where possible, find or trap the pest itself.

lessons.title: Identification methods and their use in control
lessons.html:
Getting the identification right

Correct identification to at least the level needed for control decisions is essential. A German cockroach infestation requires a very different approach from an American cockroach problem; a primary grain pest indicates a different risk from a secondary one; drywood termites require different treatment from subterranean termites.

Methods

  1. Visual identification of adults using key features: size, colour, shape, antennae, wings and markings. A hand lens is essential for stored product insects.
  2. Identification keys and guides, including industry reference guides and pictorial keys.
  3. Monitoring devices: pheromone traps capture specific moth or beetle species; sticky traps indicate cockroach species and hot spots; insect light traps show flying insect profiles.
  4. Specimen submission to a specialist or laboratory when identification is uncertain or regulatory consequences depend on it, for example suspected quarantine pests in export consignments.

Handling specimens

Collect specimens in sealed, labelled vials with date, site and exact location. Keep insects in alcohol or dry as the receiving laboratory requests. Photograph specimens with a scale reference.

Linking identification to action

Identification tells youExample
Where to treatGerman cockroaches harbour in warm kitchen equipment
Which stage to targetWood borer larvae inside timber need a penetrating treatment
Which product is registeredThe label lists specific target pests
Risk levelRodents in food areas pose disease and contamination risk
Client actionsMoisture correction for decay fungi

Key points

  • Life cycle, habits and needs of a pest determine where, when and how to control it.
  • Hidden stages such as larvae inside kernels or timber are protected from contact treatments.
  • Recognise pests from signs: holes, frass, webbing, droppings, smears, mud tubes and odours.
  • Confirm that evidence is fresh before concluding there is current activity.
  • Use hand lens, keys, traps and laboratory submission to confirm identification before choosing a registered treatment.
